1.goal: To open the lesson on a moment from her own work when a question caught her unprepared, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Ask whether she did the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she gives a short turnover update on a call, and you interrupt her with questions.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you listen to a call where two directors interrupt a presentation. Then you give an update, and I interrupt you.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of one meeting. Who asked, and what did you answer?”
1.expected: One episode in two or three sentences: who asked, what the question was, and what she did. A complete answer looks like “In a meeting with my boss in the US, she asked me why the number was different from last month, and I did not have the report with me.” Any episode she brings is right here.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, offer two kinds of moment: a question about a number, or a question in a presentation.
1.challenge: Ask what she would say now, in that same moment.
1.monitoring: Whether she describes the question itself or only how she felt.
1.evidence: The episode she brings, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has told one episode.

2.goal: To establish who is on the call, what Renata prepared, and what she did not.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her. The company is the one from the article in the last lesson.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer.
2.expected: Something close to “How the cost was calculated, and whether it is real money.” Any answer about the cost, its source or how sure it is works here. It is her prediction from her own experience; the call answers it later.
2.support: If she does not remember the article, say in one sentence what it was about: a closed shipping route, 12-hour shifts at Norvale’s largest site, and people leaving it.
2.challenge: Ask what an operations director would want to know that a finance director would not.
2.monitoring: Whether she draws on her experience of reporting to directors in the US.
2.transition: Move on when she has answered the question on screen.

3.goal: To have her commit to three guesses before she listens, so the first listening has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer on each and leave them unconfirmed: the call settles them.
exact: Before moving on: “Those are your guesses. Now we listen and see.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open. For your reference, the call will show the directors asking about the turnover figure and the cost, interrupting Renata, and Alison asking what HR needs to bring the number down.
3.support: If she hesitates, ask her to answer as if she were Renata, preparing for the call.
3.challenge: Ask which question she would least like to be asked on that call.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess or waits to be told.
3.evidence: Her three guesses, kept for screen 4.
3.transition: Move on when all three questions have an answer.

4.goal: To follow the whole call once for the general picture: who asks the questions and how the call ends.
4.interaction: S listens alone, then T–S on the two questions.
run: Read the two questions with her before you press Play.
Play the call once, at Normal.
Take her answers, and then ask which of her guesses from screen 3 the call confirms. Keep the transcript for the next screen.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Listen once, all the way through. Find the answers to these two questions.”
4.expected: Alison and Greg both ask Renata questions, and she answers all of them; one of them she checks before answering. At the end Renata asks for “a decision on the shift model before the end of the month.”
4.support: If she lost track of who is who, play it once at Slower and ask only the first question.
4.challenge: Ask which of Greg's questions was the hardest one for Renata, and why.
4.monitoring: Whether she follows the whole call or stops at a number she did not catch.
4.evidence: How much of the call she followed in one listening without support.
4.transition: Move on when both questions have an answer, even a partial one.

5.goal: To separate what the call actually says from what sounds likely, and to go back to the line to prove it.
5.interaction: S listens and says which statements are true; T marks them on screen. Then T–S with the transcript.
run: Play the call again. For each statement, she says true or false and you mark her choice on screen. When three are marked, press Check.
Then go through the six out loud. On each, open the transcript and ask her to find the line.
Spend the time that is left on the cost per exit.
exact: On each statement: “Where does the call say that? Find the line.”
On the cost per exit: “Renata says a number for each exit. Did the company pay that number?”
5.expected: True: “Turnover at Guarulhos went up to 14.6%.” (“went from nine point two to fourteen point six percent”) · “Forty-eight people left in three months.” · “Greg wants to know how the total was calculated.” (“How you get to it.”). False: “Most of the cost appears as one line in the budget.” — Renata says “you won't see it as one line in the budget” · “Renata gives Greg a cost per exit that the company actually paid.” — it is “an estimate of about four thousand eight hundred seventy dollars per exit” · “Renata has already decided on a new shift model.” — she asks for a decision on it.
5.support: If one will not come, play only the part of the call it depends on.
5.challenge: Ask which of the false statements Greg could repeat in a board meeting by mistake.
5.monitoring: Whether she separates what was said from what she knows about turnover from her own work.
5.evidence: Which false statement she said was true, if any.
5.transition: Move on when the six are settled and the cost per exit has been discussed.

6.goal: To hear five questions from the call again and decide what each one wants from the person who answers.
6.interaction: S listens to the two parts and says what each question wants; T chooses it on screen. Then T–S.
run: Play The cost and The end of the call once each.
For each of the five questions, she says what it wants and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through them. Spend the time on the two questions that ask the listener to choose, and on break that down.
exact: On break that down: “Greg says ‘break that down’. What are the two things he could want?”
6.expected: To hear a number again: “Was that fourteen or forty?” To get an explanation: “Can you break that down for me?” To choose between two things: “Is that money we actually spent, or money we lost?” · “Do you mean the total, or how we get to the total?” To find out what someone needs: “What would you need from us to bring it down?” The two meanings of break that down are the total in its parts, or how the total was reached.
6.support: On each question, ask: what does the person want to have after the answer?
6.challenge: Ask her to turn “Can you break that down for me?” into a question that cannot be misread.
6.monitoring: Whether she hears the questions at normal speed or needs the transcript.
6.evidence: What she said break that down could mean.
6.transition: Move on when the five are classified.

7.goal: To have her notice how Renata checks an ambiguous question before answering it, and to hear the forms of the check.
run: Read the three lines and the question on screen with her.
Let her answer both parts of the question before you open the button.
Open what she did and read it with her. Then ask her for one check of her own about something from her work.
exact: If she does not see it: “If Renata had just given the total, what would Greg have said?”
Asking for her own check: “Somebody asks you: ‘Is turnover high?’ Check it before you answer.”
7.expected: Renata does not give a number: she names two meanings of Greg's question, the total or how they get to the total, and lets him choose. If she had answered straight away with the total, Greg would have had to ask again, because he wanted the calculation. From the reveal: “Just so I answer the right question, do you mean… or…?”, “Are you asking about… or about…?”, and “Let me think about that for a second.” when the question is clear and the answer is not ready. Her own check can be as short as “Compared with what: last year, or the market?”.
7.support: Cover Renata's line, ask what she would answer to Greg, then uncover it.
7.challenge: Ask her for a check that names two time periods instead of two kinds of answer.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the check before the reveal, and whether her own check names two real meanings.
7.evidence: Her own check, word for word.
7.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has made one check of her own.

8.goal: To make the check out loud, quickly, in response to short questions about her work that can mean two things.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one question at a time.
run: Play the five sentences one at a time, and ask her to say each one after it. The words of each sentence stay hidden.
Open the words of a sentence with Show the words only if she needs to read it after two listens, and close them before the next sentence.
Tell her she can use the examples she heard when she checks your questions. Then ask the questions below, one at a time. Before each answer, she checks what you mean.
After her check, choose one meaning and let her answer it in one or two sentences.
exact: Question 1: “Is your turnover high?”
Question 2: “How much does it cost when someone leaves?”
Question 3: “Has absenteeism gone up?”
Question 4: “Can you break down your team for me?”
8.expected: A check that names two meanings, then an answer to the one you chose. Possible checks: for question 1, “Compared with what: last year, or the market?”; for question 2, “Are you asking about the direct cost, or the total with lost productivity?”; for question 3, “Do you mean this quarter, or the whole year?”; for question 4, “Do you mean how many people, or who does what?”. Any check that names two real meanings is correct.
8.support: If the check does not come, say its first words — “Just so I answer the right question…” — and let her finish it.
8.challenge: Ask a question that is clear, and see whether she answers without checking. Checking every question is not the goal.
8.monitoring: Whether the check names two real meanings, and how long it takes her to start it.
8.evidence: How many of the four she checked without help.
8.transition: Move on when she has checked and answered the four questions.

9.goal: To give a short turnover update on a call and handle interruptions: checking the ambiguous question, saying a number again, and going back to the update.
9.interaction: Role-play. You are a colleague from work on the call, and you interrupt her with some questions; she gives the update.
run: Read the two options and the list on screen with her, and let her choose. For option A, give her a moment to decide her figures.
Let her start the update. After her first figure, interrupt with the number question. Later, interrupt with the ambiguous question.
Wait for the check before you clarify. Then choose a meaning and let her answer.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, and close them again. Leave corrections for screen 11.
exact: After a number: “Sorry, was that nine or nineteen?” (option B) / “Sorry, did you say fifteen or fifty?” — use one of her own numbers (option A)
The ambiguous question: “Is that a lot?”
When she checks, choose: “Compared with the other site.” (option B) / “Compared with last year.” (option A)
At the end: “What would it take to bring it down?”
9.expected: The update with its figures said in full (for option B: “At Campinas, turnover went from six point eight to nine point one percent in the second quarter. Twenty-three people left. At about four thousand eight hundred seventy dollars per exit, that is roughly one hundred twelve thousand dollars.”), the number said again with the stress or the digits (“Nine. Nine point one, not nineteen.”), a check before answering “Is that a lot?” (“Compared with what: the other site, or last year?”), an answer to the meaning you chose (option B: lower than Guarulhos, which went to 14.6%), and the update picked up again. The last question has no fixed answer; any concrete request, marked as hers, is correct.
9.support: If she answers “Is that a lot?” without checking, say nothing, and ask it again the same way. If she still answers straight away, point at the second item on the list.
9.challenge: If she checks cleanly, ask one question that sounds clear and is not: “And the people who left, were they good?”
9.monitoring: Whether the check comes before the answer, and what she does in the first seconds after each interruption.
9.evidence: The option she chose, whether she checked “Is that a lot?”, and one of her answers written word for word. It goes into the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has handled the three interruptions and finished the update.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after the call: answer two questions from a colleague, checking the one that can mean two things, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are a colleague from work, calling her after the call.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. Give her time to add a reason.
Then ask her to put one question to you about what you need from HR, and answer it.
exact: Question 1: “What worries you more about those numbers?”
Question 2: “If we do nothing, where will that number be at the end of the year?”
Handing the turn over: “Anything you need from me?”
10.expected: Two answers with a reason, and one question from her. Question 1 can mean the turnover figure or the cost, so a complete answer may start with a check (“Do you mean the turnover itself, or what it costs?”) and then gives a reason: “What worries me more is the turnover at the largest site, because it went up by more than half in one quarter.” Question 2 has no answer in the figures, so any projection marked as her reading is correct (“My reading is that it will keep going up while the shifts stay the same.”). Her question can be as small as “When will the decision on the shifts be made?”.
10.support: If she answers without a reason, ask “Why that one?” and wait.
10.challenge: Disagree once: “I think the cost number is too soft to use.” Let her answer you.
10.monitoring: Whether she checks the first question without being prompted, and whether she stays in English.
10.evidence: Whether she checked, whether she gave reasons without being asked, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the update again from the other option, with a question she has not heard.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the answer you noted on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. The two options are on screen again: read the option she did not choose with her. She gives the update from that option, and you ask the new question below.
exact: The new question: “And how does that compare?”
If she checks, choose: “With the market.”
11.expected: The update from the other option, with the figures said in full, a check before answering “And how does that compare?” (“Compared with the other site, or with the market?”), and an answer to the meaning you chose. If she has no market figure, a complete answer says so: “I do not have the market figure here. I can send it after the call.”
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Add a second question she has not heard, and let her go back to the update after it.
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve changed in the second version.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when someone asks you a question that can mean two things, name the two before you answer.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: following the call, hearing numbers that sound alike, telling what a question wants, checking an ambiguous question, asking for and saying a number again, going back to the update, and answering a colleague’s questions after the call. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one check she made today.
12.challenge: Ask where she expects the first ambiguous question this week.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is about the verb that the time period needs when you talk about a number.
